terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run the clipboard here to see this morning's count.

tasks.title: Name the crossing
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `Clipboard.java`, make a `String` called `crossing` that holds the text `Lanternquay to Corran`. Then print it.

Check compiles and runs your Task 1 lines and reads `crossing`: it must be a `String` holding exactly that text, and the program must print it.
nextSteps: Find `// Task 1` in the file.
Write the type, the name, `=`, the text in double quotes and a semicolon.
Print it with `System.out.println` on the next line, using the variable's name.
Run `java Clipboard.java` and read the output.
hints: A variable is made with a type, a name and a value. The lesson makes one for a kettle.
The type for text is `String`, with a capital S. The text goes in double quotes.
The line has the shape `String crossing = "...";`, then `System.out.println(crossing);` under it.

tasks.title: Count the seats left
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make an `int` called `seatsLeft`. It starts with the number of seats on the boat, which is in `seats` near the top of the file. Then print it.

Check runs your Task 2 lines with other numbers in place of the ones at the top, so `seatsLeft` has to be built on the name `seats`, not on a number you type.
nextSteps: Read the two lines under "This morning's numbers".
Under `// Task 2`, make `seatsLeft` with the type for whole numbers.
Give it the value of `seats` by writing that name on the right of `=`.
Print it and run the program.
hints: A variable can start with the value of another variable, not only with a number you type.
A count of seats is a whole number, which tells you the type. On the right of `=`, write the name of the variable that holds the seats.
The line has the shape `int seatsLeft = ...;`, with the seats' variable name where the dots are.

tasks.title: Board the passengers
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, `boarded` passengers just got on. Give `seatsLeft` a new value: the seats left after they board. Then print it again.

Check runs your Task 2 and Task 3 lines with other numbers at the top and reads `seatsLeft` at the end. It also reads your Task 3 lines to see that they give the existing variable a new value rather than making a new one.
nextSteps: Make sure Task 2 passes first: Task 3 changes the same variable.
Under `// Task 3`, start a line with the name `seatsLeft` and `=`.
On the right, take `boarded` away from the seats left now.
Print it again and run the program: you should see two different counts.
hints: You are not making a new variable here. You are changing one you already made.
Giving a variable a new value is its name, `=` and the new value, with no type in front. The right side can use the variable's own current value.
The line has the shape `seatsLeft = seatsLeft - ...;`, with the boarded passengers' variable where the dots are.

tasks.title: Write down the fare
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, make a `double` called `fare` that holds `3.20`, the price of a single crossing in pounds. Then print it.

Check compiles and runs your Task 4 lines and reads `fare`: it must be a `double` holding that price, and the program must print it.
nextSteps: Find `// Task 4` and read which type the task asks for.
Make `fare` with that type and the price, written with a point.
Print it and run the program.
Compare what it prints with what you wrote: the lesson says why it looks a little different.
hints: A price has a part after the point, so it needs a type that can hold one.
`int` holds whole numbers only, and the compiler refuses to squeeze `3.20` into one. `double` holds numbers with a point.
The line has the shape `double fare = ...;`, with the price where the dots are.

tasks.title: Give a and b real names
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 5`, two variables are called `a` and `b`, and nobody can tell what they hold. Rename `a` to `skipper` and `b` to `boatName`, everywhere they appear. Their values stay the same.

Check compiles and runs your Task 5 lines, reads `skipper` and `boatName`, makes sure `a` and `b` are gone, and looks for the same two lines in the output as before.
nextSteps: Read the four lines under `// Task 5`.
Rename `a` where it is made.
Rename it where it is used too, then do the same for `b`.
Run the program: it should print the same two lines as before.
hints: A variable's name appears where it is made and everywhere it is used.
If you rename it in one place only, the compiler says `cannot find symbol` and names the one it no longer knows. Read it: it tells you which line to fix.
Four places change: the two lines that make `a` and `b`, and the two lines that print them.
